22 What are the SI base units of stress?
A
kg m s–2
B
kg m–1
s–2
C
kg m–2
s–2
D
kg m–3
s–2

hints: Recall the definition of stress used for a stretched wire: stress equals force divided by cross-sectional area.
Write force in SI base units from $F = ma$ as $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$ and area as $\text{m}^2$.
Divide the base units of force by $\text{m}^2$ and combine the powers of $\text{m}$ to find the power of metre in stress.
walkthrough: Start from the definition: stress $= \frac{force}{area}$ with unit $\text{N m}^{-2}$ or pascal.
Express the newton in SI base units using $F = ma$: $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg} \times 1 \text{ m s}^{-2} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$.
Express area in base units as $\text{m}^2$.
Substitute: unit of stress $= \frac{\text{kg m s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^2} = \text{kg m}^{1-2}\text{s}^{-2} = \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}$.
Check against the options: only the option with $\text{kg}$ to power 1, $\text{m}$ to power -1 and $\text{s}$ to power -2 matches. This is option B.

A.explanation: This is the base-unit form of force, $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$. Stress divides force by area so an extra $\text{m}^{-2}$ is missing.

B.explanation: Force per unit area gives $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$ divided by $\text{m}^2$, which simplifies to $\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}$.

C.explanation: This has one power of $\text{m}$ too many in the denominator and would correspond to force divided by volume, not area.

D.explanation: This has two powers of $\text{m}$ too many in the denominator and does not match force divided by area.
